posts.title: Freezing level inside a cloud layer
posts.headline: In cloud, you cross the freezing level without seeing it.
posts.alt: Freezing level inside a cloud layer: an illustrated diagram for pilots. In cloud, you cross the freezing level without seeing it. The picture shows one thick continuous cloud layer that clearly spans both above and below the freezing level; a thin dashed horizontal freezing-level line crossing through the inside of the cloud, not at its base or top; a ghost aircraft, pale and translucent, inside the cloud below the freezing line; the solid aircraft inside the same cloud, above the freezing line. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Where does the freezing level sit when you're climbing through cloud?

Structural icing needs visible moisture and an airframe at or below freezing, and a cold-soaked airframe can be below freezing in air that is not. A climb through one layer can cross the freezing level while you're still inside the cloud, with the same moisture around you. Nothing outside looks different.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Structural icing needs visible moisture and an airframe surface at or below freezing, and a cold-soaked airframe can be below freezing in air that is not.
A climb through a cloud layer can cross a freezing level inside the cloud.
Below a front, rain from warmer air above can fall into below-freezing air, become supercooled, and freeze on impact with an aircraft.
Icing in freezing precipitation often covers a broad area, and a pilot may be unable to escape it by descending.
posts.intent: Cloud and sub-zero temperature are two separate conditions, and structural ice needs both, so the climb is the decision.

article.heading: Why ice needs cloud and cold together
paragraphs: Picture a climb out through a solid overcast with the ground falling away. You are wet the whole way up, but moisture alone does not make ice.

Structural icing, the ice that builds on the outside of the airframe, needs two things at the same time. One is visible moisture, such as cloud or rain. The other is an airframe surface at or below freezing.

For the air, the handbooks are plain about it. The outside air temperature, or OAT, has to be below 0 °C for icing to happen. There is one exception, covered further down, because the airframe does not always match the air.

Ice matters because of what it does to airflow, far more than its weight. Frost or ice no rougher than coarse sandpaper on the leading edge or top of the wing can cut lift by 30 percent. That same thin layer can raise drag by up to 40 percent, and bigger buildups by 80 percent or more.

article.heading: Where the freezing level hides in cloud
paragraphs: The freezing level is the height where the air temperature passes through 0 °C. Higher air is typically colder, which is why the handbooks list temperature and altitude together.
A cloud layer does not stop at the freezing level. One layer can straddle it, with its lower part in air above zero and its upper part in air below.
Climb through that layer and you cross the line while still inside the cloud. The moisture around you is the same before and after. Only the temperature changed, and the cloud gives no sign of it.
That makes the climb itself the decision. Below the line, the cloud supplies moisture and the air is above freezing. Above it, the cloud supplies both ingredients at once.

article.heading: How cold the icing band usually is
paragraphs: Passing 0 °C does not mean more ice with every degree. Clouds hold supercooled water, liquid drops colder than freezing, and the colder the cloud gets, the less of it there is. Eventually only ice crystals remain.
That is why icing bunches into a band of temperature and height. High stratiform cloud colder than -20 °C is mostly ice crystals and gives little icing. The table shows where the reports gather.

Temperature also shapes the kind of ice. Rime, the rough milky kind, tends to form colder than -15 °C, and mixed ice forms between that and -10 °C. Clear ice, glossy and hard to see, tends to form warmer than -10 °C.
So the first degrees past the freezing level are clear ice territory. The handbooks call this general guidance, since drop size, water content and the aircraft itself change the result.

rows: The only physical cold limit, where liquid drops freeze on their own

article.heading: When the airframe is colder than the air
paragraphs: Say you have been flying in cold air and then descend into air above 0 °C. The airframe does not warm up to the air temperature straight away.
This is called cold soaking. A cold-soaked airframe can stay below 0 °C for some time, and on some aircraft it stays that cold even after landing.
Aircraft with fuel tanks mounted flush to the skin are especially prone to this. They can pick up ice in air only slightly above 0 °C.
So an OAT reading just above zero is not a clean bill of health in cloud. How long an airframe holds the cold varies from type to type, so know your own aircraft's limits.

article.heading: Why the top of a layer ices most
paragraphs: Flat, layered cloud is called stratiform. In low and middle stratiform layers, icing on average sits in a band 3,000 to 4,000 ft thick, and it usually runs from trace to light.
The strongest icing in these layers is in the upper part of the cloud. In a climb where the freezing level sits mid-layer, that upper part is exactly where you arrive after crossing it.
The shallow band helps you. A change of only a few thousand feet may take you out of the icing, even while you stay in cloud. The catch is that these layers spread a very long way sideways.

Heaped cloud, called cumuliform, is built differently. Its icing is narrower but taller, and in a building cloud it runs through every level above the freezing level. It is worst near the top, where the updraft is concentrated.

article.heading: When descending does not get you out
paragraphs: Going down to warmer air has a trap near fronts, which is where most icing reports come from. Under a front, air above freezing can sit on top of a layer below freezing.
Rain forms up in the warm air and falls into the cold layer underneath. The drops cool below freezing but stay liquid, which makes them supercooled. They freeze the moment they strike an aircraft.

This is a favoured spot for severe clear icing, because there is so much supercooled water. If the cold layer is shallow, the rain reaches the ground as freezing rain. If it is deep, the drops freeze into ice pellets, and ice pellets mean icing above.
Freezing rain often covers a broad area. With the cold air underneath you, a pilot may be unable to escape it by descending.

figure.caption: Rain made in the warm air above the front turns supercooled in the cold wedge below it, and that wedge is where the aircraft is.
figure.alt: Rain made in the warm air above the front turns supercooled in the cold wedge below it, and that wedge is where the aircraft is.

article.heading: What to do when ice starts
paragraphs: Whatever ice protection your aircraft has, the first move is to leave the visible moisture. That could mean descending below the cloud bases, climbing above the tops, or turning onto a different course.
If none of those is possible, move to an altitude where the temperature is above freezing. Under freezing rain that may not work, and near mountains the terrain may stop you from descending to it.
Ice also feeds itself once it starts. Adding power and raising the nose to hold altitude increases the angle of attack, and that lets ice collect on the underside of the wings and fuselage.

posts.title: Carburettor ice on a warm day
posts.headline: Your carburettor makes its own cold, whatever the OAT.
posts.alt: Carburettor ice on a warm day: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your carburettor makes its own cold, whatever the OAT. The picture shows a rendered single-engine aeroplane in level cruise, small and high in the frame, over hazy summer farmland; a large cutaway of its carburettor filling the near foreground, sectioned along the induction path so intake mouth, venturi throat and throttle plate all read; pale streamlines entering the intake mouth and squeezing through the narrow throat, with the fuel spray leaving the nozzle in that same throat; a granular rime collar around the partly closed throttle plate, feathering thinner up the bore wall behind it. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: How does carburettor ice form when the outside air is well above freezing?

Fuel vaporising in the venturi absorbs heat, and the pressure drop through it cools the induction air further. The charge can end up below freezing. A warm OAT is what makes the risk easy to dismiss, and reduced power in humid air is when it shows up.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Fuel vaporisation and the pressure drop through the venturi cool the induction air substantially below ambient.
Carburettor ice is therefore possible at outside air temperatures well above freezing, particularly at high humidity and reduced power.
posts.intent: The temperature drop happens inside the carburettor, so ice forms on a day well above freezing.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 7

article.heading: Where the cold comes from
paragraphs: Picture a warm, muggy afternoon and a long stretch at low power. The air you are flying through feels nothing like icing weather. Inside the engine, though, the air is about to get colder.

That air first enters the carburettor, the part that mixes fuel into the air before it reaches the cylinders. It flows down the bore, the tube the air travels through, and into the venturi. The venturi is a narrow throat in that tube.
Two things happen in the throat. The air speeds up and its pressure drops. At the same point, fuel sprays from a nozzle and turns from liquid into vapour.
Both steps take heat out of the air. So the air leaving the venturi is colder than the air outside the aeroplane. Everything else in this article follows from that one fact.

article.heading: Why a pressure drop cools the air
paragraphs: You have met this effect before, in weather. A parcel of air that rises moves into lower pressure and expands. Expanding takes energy, and that energy comes out of the air as heat.

The FAA's Aviation Weather handbook, AC 00-6B, gives the rate for the atmosphere. Dry rising air cools approximately 3 °C per 1,000 feet. That rate is called the dry adiabatic lapse rate, adiabatic meaning no heat moves in or out of the parcel.

The venturi works on the same idea, only across a few inches of metal instead of thousands of feet. The source gives no figure for how far the air cools there. Take the lapse rate as proof of the physics, and don't treat it as a measure of the carburettor.
Fuel vaporising adds a second drop on top. Liquid fuel needs heat to become vapour. It takes that heat from the air right around the spray.

article.heading: Where the water in the ice comes from
paragraphs: Ice needs water. Humid air carries plenty of it as vapour you cannot see. The dewpoint is the temperature at which that air would be saturated, holding all the vapour it can.
When air cools, its temperature falls toward its dewpoint. The gap between the two is the temperature-dewpoint spread. As the spread closes, the relative humidity climbs.
AC 00-6B works an example. A parcel starts at 18 °C with a dewpoint of 13 °C. It cools 3 °C per 1,000 feet as it rises while its dewpoint falls only 0.5 °C, so it saturates at 2,000 feet.

Once air is saturated, more cooling forces water out of it. In the sky that water becomes cloud. In the carburettor throat, it is the moisture that freezes onto the throttle plate in the picture above.

table.caption: How an air parcel's temperature, dewpoint and humidity change as it moves, from AC 00-6B Table 11-1.

article.heading: Why a warm day still allows ice
paragraphs: Your outside air temperature, the OAT, describes the air outside the cowling. It tells you nothing direct about the air in the venturi. That air has already been cooled on its way in.

The temperature that matters is the one inside the carburettor. That is why carburettor ice is possible with the OAT well above freezing. The warm number on the gauge is measured in the wrong place for this problem.
This is also what makes carburettor ice easy to miss. A warm day feels like the wrong day for it. A pilot who judges the risk by the OAT alone may never think of it at all.

article.heading: When the risk is highest
paragraphs: Two conditions raise the risk most. The first is high humidity, and the section on dewpoint explains why. Moist air already sits close to its dewpoint, so it takes less cooling to reach saturation.
The second is reduced power. The throttle controls the flow of fuel and air to the engine through the throttle plate, a flap across the bore. At a low power setting that plate sits partly closed.

The picture above shows what that costs you. Ice builds on the edge of the plate and shrinks the gap the air still has. Put humid air and a low power setting together and you have the conditions the risk favours.

article.heading: Humidity and low power are not limits
paragraphs: Read the wording closely. Carburettor ice is possible particularly at high humidity and reduced power. Particularly marks the most likely cases and leaves the rest open.
Drier air or a higher power setting lowers the odds. Neither one rules ice out. Treat those conditions as the likely cases, and never as the only ones.
The source gives no temperature range and no humidity figure that marks a safe day. Without one, a warm OAT and a dry feel to the air are no reason to stop thinking about it.

posts.title: Acceleration that feels like a climb
posts.headline: With nothing to see outside, speeding up feels like pitching up.
posts.alt: Acceleration that feels like a climb: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With nothing to see outside, speeding up feels like pitching up. The picture shows a rendered Cessna 172 in clean left profile, seen level and square to its flank, high wing with visible struts and fixed tricycle gear, its nose pitched clearly down below level; a translucent outline of the same aeroplane overlapping it and sharing its tail position, pitched clearly nose-high, so the picture reads as one aeroplane in two attitudes rather than as two aircraft; a wide, obvious angle between the two noses, the ghost's high and the solid one's low, which is the subject of the picture; a thin pale line tracing the aeroplane's real path: up off the runway, over a shallow crest, then bending down toward the unlit water. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Why does forward acceleration feel like a nose-up pitch attitude?

Accelerate forward with no outside references and your sense of pitch says the nose came up. It did not, and the correction it invites is lowering the nose toward the surface. Nothing outside can settle it, so fly the pitch on the flight instruments and disregard what your body is reporting.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Forward acceleration can produce a false sensation of a nose-up pitch attitude.
Without outside visual references the pilot may lower the nose toward the surface, so pitch must be flown on the flight instruments rather than on what the body reports.
posts.intent: On a dark night takeoff, acceleration pushes the inner ear the same way a nose-up pitch would, and the instinct is to push down.

article.heading: What happens on a dark night takeoff
paragraphs: Picture a night takeoff toward open water. You add full power, the aeroplane gathers speed, and the runway lights slide away behind you. Ahead of the windscreen there is nothing to look at.
Somewhere in the roll or the first part of the climb, your body tells you the nose has come up. It feels steep. The aeroplane has not pitched up at all.
The instinct that follows is to ease the stick forward and bring the nose down. That is the trap. The rest of this page walks through where the feeling comes from and why the answer is on the panel.

article.heading: Why speeding up feels like tilting back
paragraphs: Your inner ear holds the otolith organs. They are the part of your balance system that senses which way gravity and acceleration are pulling on your head.

Tilt your head backwards and the otolith organs register the change. A hard shove forward, like the one you get on a takeoff roll, stimulates them in the same way. From that signal alone, your brain cannot tell the two apart.
So it reports the familiar story. You feel yourself tilting back, which in an aeroplane means nose-up. This false sense of a raised nose from speeding up is called the somatogravic illusion.
The handbook uses takeoff as its example, because that is where a rapid acceleration is part of every flight. You meet the conditions for it every time you open the throttle.

figure.caption: Tilting your head back and speeding up forward send your inner ear the same message.
figure.alt: Tilting your head back and speeding up forward send your inner ear the same message.

article.heading: Why a dark night makes it worse
paragraphs: In daylight your eyes settle the question. You glance out, see the horizon where it should be, and know the nose is where you put it.

The illusion is most likely when visual references are poor. Over open water at night, black water meets black sky with no seam, and there is nothing to check the feeling against. The handbook names that exact case as flight without a visible horizon.
It lumps marginal visibility in with it, meaning visibility of less than 3 miles. In either case the inner ear becomes the loudest voice left in the cockpit.

Seat of the pants flying will not save you here. That means judging attitude from the pressure you feel through your seat, skin and muscles. Acceleration forces can overpower gravity, and then those signals go false as well.

article.heading: What the wrong correction does
paragraphs: Convinced the nose is high, a disoriented pilot pushes forward. The handbook says this can put the aeroplane into a nose-low attitude, or into a dive.
Just after takeoff you have very little height to give away. Lowering the nose there points the aeroplane at the surface you just left, while your body still insists you are climbing.

The illusion also runs in reverse. Pull the throttle back quickly and the rapid slowdown can have the opposite effect. The disoriented pilot then pulls the nose up, toward a nose-high attitude or a stall.

Pushes into a nose-low or dive attitude

article.heading: How to feel it safely with an instructor
paragraphs: You can meet this illusion on purpose. The handbook describes a demonstration called climbing while accelerating.

You close your eyes. Your instructor holds approach speed, straight and level, for several seconds. Then they speed up while keeping the aeroplane straight and level, and the usual sensation is that you are climbing.

A second exercise gets the same feeling from a turn. The instructor rolls slowly into a coordinated turn of about 1.5 positive G, approximately 50° of bank, and holds it for 90°. G is the load pressing you into your seat, and here it reads as a climb too.

Both exercises prove the same point. Your body's sense of attitude is often wrong, while the instruments are not fooled. Do them only at a safe height, with an instructor or a suitable safety pilot aboard.

article.heading: How to fly pitch on the instruments
paragraphs: Take pitch from the flight instruments, and treat what your body reports as noise. On a dark takeoff, set the attitude you want on the panel and hold it there. If the nose feels like it is climbing away, check the instruments before you touch the stick.

The false feeling is normal, and no amount of training makes it go away completely. What training does is teach you to override it. The more instrument flying you do, the less these illusions pull on you.
Get that training before you need it. The handbook says to get it before flying in visibility under 3 miles. The same goes for anywhere without a visible horizon, such as over open water at night.

Keep your head still during the takeoff, since sudden head movement is on the handbook's list of things to avoid. Arrive rested, too. Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, lost sleep and mild hypoxia, a shortage of oxygen, all make you easier to fool.

posts.title: Rotor cloud under a mountain wave
posts.headline: In a mountain wave, the roughest low-level air is under that smooth cloud.
posts.alt: Rotor cloud under a mountain wave: an illustrated diagram for pilots. In a mountain wave, the roughest low-level air is under that smooth cloud. The picture shows a mountain ridge in profile with the wind crossing it left to right; a smooth, hard-edged lens of lenticular cloud sitting at the wave crest downwind of the summit; a torn, ragged rotor cloud directly below that lenticular, at about ridge-top height; streamlines drawn unbroken from the lenticular down into the rotor, so the two clouds read as one wave. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: What's the difference between a lenticular cloud and a rotor cloud?

Air crossing a ridge can set up a standing wave downwind. Smooth lenticular cloud marks the crests. The rotor turns underneath, and down low that roll is usually the roughest part. The wave can be rough higher up too, so smooth cloud above is not a promise of smooth air.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: A mountain wave is often marked by lenticular and rotor clouds, but extremely severe wave winds can occur with little or no visual warning.
Mountain waves are mechanical turbulence above and downwind of mountains, and they can bring turbulence of potentially destructive intensity.
Both vertically propagating mountain waves and trapped lee waves can be hazardous to aviation operations.
posts.intent: The smooth lenticular above and the ragged rotor below belong to the same wave, and down low the rotor is where the turbulence lives.

figure_key.label: ROTOR: USUALLY THE ROUGHEST

article.heading: How a ridge sets the air bouncing
paragraphs: Picture a strong wind blowing straight across a ridge. The air has to go up and over, and what it does next depends on how stable it is.
Stable air is air that resists being pushed up or down. Lift it over the ridge and it ends up heavier than the air around it. Gravity pulls it back toward the level it came from.

It doesn't stop at that level. Its momentum carries it lower, where it warms as it's squeezed and becomes lighter than the air around it. So it rises again, overshoots again, and keeps swinging until the motion dies out.

That swinging is a gravity wave, a wave driven by gravity pulling displaced air back into place. You need both parts. With a weak wind the ridge can act like a dam and hold the air back, and unstable air builds deep convective clouds or thunderstorms instead of a wave.

article.heading: Two kinds of wave, both a hazard
paragraphs: The wave behind a ridge takes one of two main forms. In a vertically propagating mountain wave, the wave's energy travels upward. The wave stands above the mountain and leans into the wind as it climbs.

In a trapped lee wave, wind shear above ridge level holds the energy down. Wind shear is a sharp change in wind speed or direction with height. The wave runs downwind of the mountain instead, stays fairly low and doesn't lean.
The handbook treats both kinds as hazardous to aviation. They can exist at the same time, and they can blend into a wave that is only partly trapped.

For a vertically propagating wave, having a wave at all isn't the problem. The danger depends on how strong it is and whether part of it breaks into turbulent motion. At the extreme, that breaking can damage or fail part of the aircraft.

article.heading: What a lenticular cloud is telling you
paragraphs: Trapped lee waves often show up as a train of altocumulus standing lenticular clouds, lens-shaped clouds downwind of the mountains. They form fairly straight bands parallel to the range, with clear gaps between them.
Depending on how the moisture is layered upwind, they can stack in several layers. That stacked, polished look is what makes them easy to trust.
Don't trust it. The handbook says these clouds can look turbulent or smooth. A clean edge shows you where the wave is, and it says nothing about how rough the air is.
These waves matter for takeoff, landing and en route flight below FL250. Down at those lower altitudes, trapped lee waves can give you strong turbulence.

article.heading: Where the rotor cloud comes from
paragraphs: When a vertically propagating wave breaks high above the ridge, it often drives very strong wind down the lee slope. That's the downwind side of the mountain. The handbook gives gusts reaching 100 kt there, a low-level turbulence hazard for every aircraft.
That fast downslope wind often stops abruptly in a jump. The jump sits some distance down the lee slope, or well downwind of the mountains.
The jump region is frequently an area of extreme turbulence. It reaches 10,000 ft or more above the surface. A strong shear layer at the jump is one source of that turbulence.
A line of ragged rotor clouds sometimes marks the jump, and those clouds churn visibly. Downwind of the jump the turbulence eases, though it can still be quite strong.

figure.caption: The rotor line sits over the jump, where the fast wind down the lee slope ends and extreme turbulence is frequent.
figure.alt: The rotor line sits over the jump, where the fast wind down the lee slope ends and extreme turbulence is frequent.

article.heading: How high each wave reaches
paragraphs: A vertically propagating wave gets stronger as it climbs, because the air thins with height. A strong inversion, a layer where temperature rises with height, or a shear layer can soak up or reflect some of that energy.

Without one, the mountain's effects can reach far above the peaks, at times beyond 60,000 ft. Where the wave breaks you get local updrafts, downdrafts and possibly sudden severe or extreme turbulence.

Trapped lee waves work the other way. They weaken with height inside the trapping layer, which usually starts within a few thousand feet of the ridge crest. When the shear layer is too weak or shallow to trap them fully, they reach higher.

Size matters too. A taller range above the land around it makes a bigger wave, and so does a stronger wind across the ridge at mountaintop level. Even modest terrain can set up an appreciable wave in the right conditions.

article.heading: When the sky gives no warning
paragraphs: These flows often come with signs you can see, such as lenticular clouds, rotor clouds or blowing dust. The handbook is clear that they don't always.
Extremely severe wind events can happen with little or no visual warning. Trapped lee waves in particular frequently occur without any cloud at all.

The most severe mountain wind events usually come when the large-scale winds are strongest, from late autumn to early spring. The rest of the year, hazardous winds near mountains are more often tied to thunderstorms and their outflow.

The eddies terrain throws off range from a few centimeters to tens or hundreds of kilometers across. Some leave you in fairly smooth air. Others bring turbulence strong enough to destroy an aircraft, and a real chance of losing control.

posts.title: The fuel you cannot use
posts.headline: Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold.
posts.alt: The fuel you cannot use: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold. The picture shows a rendered low-wing single-engine aeroplane in level cruise, solid and fully lit, with a thin pale track line running forward from the spinner and stopping in open air; a translucent dimmed ghost of the same aeroplane further along that same track line, with open air between the solid aircraft and the ghost; a cut-away section through the wing fuel tank lifted large into the near foreground, joined to the wing root by one thin line; fuel brimmed to the filler neck inside that cut-away, its upper surface clearly the top of what the tank holds. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold.
Full explainer with the FAA sources it rests on flightdecide.com/e/fuel-cannot
teaches: An aircraft's total fuel capacity includes an unusable quantity that cannot be relied on in flight.
Fuel planning uses the usable figure from the approved flight manual.
posts.intent: Usable fuel is less than total fuel, and the difference is a published number rather than a rounding error.

article.heading: Why full tanks are not full
paragraphs: You top the tanks, watch the fuel rise to the filler neck, and call them full. Full is the tanks holding all they can. Some of what is in there will never reach the engine.
Fuel leaves the tank through a pickup, an opening the fuel line feeds from. That pickup sits a short way above the floor of the tank. Fuel lying below that opening has nothing there to draw it up.
So the tank carries two quantities at the same time. Total fuel is all of it. Usable fuel is the part the engine can be fed, and it is the smaller figure.

article.heading: Why engines quit with fuel aboard
paragraphs: Between the tank and the cylinders sits a pump, and pumps are built to move liquid. Once the fuel level drops below the pickup, the pump is drawing air. The engine gets nothing it can burn.

Picture the last of it sliding along the tank floor while the propeller winds down. That is fuel starvation, fuel aboard the aircraft that never arrives at the engine. The tanks are not empty. The engine is.

Some engines are fuel injected, with the fuel sprayed in at the cylinder intake ports. Others mix it with the incoming air in a carburetor first. Neither one can use fuel the pump cannot lift out of the tank.

article.heading: Where the real number lives
paragraphs: The flight manual approved for your aircraft gives the usable figure, and that is the one you plan with. It is a published number. Somebody wrote that figure into the table for this aircraft, and it is there to be read before you fly.
Find the fuel section of the manual and read the usable figure for your aircraft. Write it down before you work out anything else. Every later number in the plan rests on that one line.

The gap between the two figures is not slack in the measurement. It is a stated quantity for that aircraft. Treat it as a rounding error and your plan ends up counting on fuel you were told not to count on.

article.heading: What this changes in your planning
paragraphs: Run the numbers against total capacity and you've spent fuel that was never yours. It does not show up early. The shortfall turns up at the end of the leg, which is the worst end to find it.

The hours you can stay up and the distance you can cover both come off the usable figure. Start from the wrong one and every line after it is wrong by the same amount. The error travels all the way to the bottom of the page.
The unusable part has weight, and you carry it the whole flight. Weight aboard costs you performance whether or not you can burn it. So it belongs in the weight you plan, not in the fuel you plan.

posts.title: Ground effect in the flare
posts.headline: Your drag falls away inside the last wingspan.
posts.alt: Ground effect in the flare: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your drag falls away inside the last wingspan. The picture shows a rendered light single nose-high in the flare, wings level, main wheels hovering a few feet above the runway centreline; a ticked vertical dimension line one wingspan tall from the low aircraft's wingtip to the asphalt, with the aeroplane sitting well inside it; ghost comparison: the same aeroplane in the same nose-high attitude, a pale unfilled outline about one and a half wingspans higher and slightly behind; tip trails behind the low aircraft pressed wide and shallow along the asphalt, while the ghost's trails curl into two deep, tight vortices. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Throttle closed, the nose where you set it, and the airplane keeps flying down the runway.
Come within a wingspan of the surface and the wing enters ground effect. Induced drag goes down. The airplane holds off, and the runway keeps going by.
The same thing happens on takeoff. You can be airborne below normal flying speed, then settle back as you climb out of the last wingspan.
FlightDecide computes your takeoff weight from the fuel you loaded.
Full explainer with the FAA sources it rests on https://flightdecide.com/explainers/ground-effect-in-the-flare/
When somebody asks why you floated, what is the one word in your answer?
teaches: Within about one wingspan of the surface, ground effect reduces induced drag and the thrust required to hold a low airspeed in level flight.
The reduced drag is why an aircraft floats in the flare and why it can lift off below normal flying speed and settle back.
posts.intent: Within about one wingspan of the surface induced drag falls away, so the aeroplane floats on air that has nowhere to go.

article.heading: What the float feels like
paragraphs: You're over the numbers at idle, easing back to hold the landing attitude. The wheels should be close to touching. Instead the airplane stays a few feet up and the runway keeps sliding by underneath.

That hold-off is ground effect. It's a change in how the wing works when it flies very close to the surface, and the handbook calls it improved performance. Near the ground the wing does the same job with less drag.

It matters most when you hold a steady attitude at low speed and low height. That happens in two places on every flight. One is the flare before touchdown, and the other is the first moments after lift-off.

article.heading: Why drag drops near the runway
paragraphs: Every wing that makes lift also makes induced drag, the drag that comes with producing lift. It's tied to the air the wing disturbs. Some air rises ahead of the wing, called upwash, and some is pushed down behind it, called downwash.

At each tip that disturbed air rolls up into wingtip vortices, the swirls that trail behind each wingtip. Close to the ground, upwash, downwash and those vortices all get weaker. Weaker vortices mean less induced drag.
Less drag means the airplane needs less thrust to hold a low airspeed in level flight. Near the surface, the same power goes further.

This only counts at low speed. At high speed, most of the total drag is parasite drag, the drag of pushing the airframe through the air. Induced drag is then a small share, so ground effect is mostly a takeoff and landing matter.

article.heading: How close the ground has to be
paragraphs: You can detect ground effect up to a height equal to one wingspan above the surface, and that's normally where it starts. Climb above that and you're out of it.
The effect grows quickly as you get lower. With the wing a quarter of a span above the surface, induced drag falls by about 25 percent. At a tenth of a span, it falls by about 50 percent.
The source gives no percentage for a full wingspan up, or for the heights in between. What its two figures do show is that the effect is strongest nearest the runway, in the last part of the descent.

table.caption: How much induced drag falls away at different wing heights above the surface.
rows: Ground effect normally occurs up to this height (no percentage given)

article.heading: Why you float in the flare
paragraphs: In the flare you're doing exactly what ground effect rewards. The power is back, the speed is low, and you're holding a steady nose-up attitude as the wing sinks toward the runway.
As the wing drops into the last wingspan, induced drag falls away. With less drag slowing it down, the airplane keeps flying longer than you expected. That extra flying is the float.
Every second of float is runway passing under you. Knowing the drag drops just where you flare means you can expect the float instead of being caught out by it.

article.heading: Why you can lift off too slow
paragraphs: The same drop in drag works on takeoff. The takeoff roll, the lift-off and the start of the climb all happen inside the ground effect area. With less drag, the airplane can seem ready to fly below the recommended airspeed.

Then it climbs past the last wingspan and loses that help. Drag and the thrust needed both go up. If you're still slow, the climb will be much weaker than at VY or even VX, the best rate and best angle of climb speeds.
That's how an airplane lifts off and then settles back. Pulling it off too early, or climbing too steeply, can put it back on the runway. Even if it stays up, the climb stays flat until you reach VX.
High density altitude, high temperature or maximum gross weight make this worse. The airplane may lift off and then be unable to climb out of ground effect or clear obstacles.

In some airplanes, flying 5 knots off the recommended speed may cut climb performance a lot. When conditions are marginal, take off at the speed your POH, the pilot's operating handbook, gives for a proper initial climb.

article.heading: What changes as you climb out
paragraphs: Down in ground effect, the static pressure around the airplane rises. That's the pressure of the surrounding air, sensed by a small port called the static source. Your airspeed indicator, altimeter and vertical speed indicator all use it.
So on the takeoff roll and just after lift-off, the airspeed indicator and altimeter read slightly lower than they should. The vertical speed indicator usually shows a descent.

As you climb out, the wing needs a higher angle of attack to keep making the same lift. Angle of attack is the angle between the wing and the oncoming air. At the same time, induced drag and thrust required both go up.
More downwash now reaches the tail. The nose tends to pitch up, and you need less elevator travel. Static pressure falls back, so indicated airspeed goes up.

article.heading: Using ground effect on purpose
paragraphs: Ground effect is a normal part of flying, and it can help you. On a long enough runway, or with no obstacles ahead, the lower drag gives you better acceleration early in the takeoff.

On a soft or rough surface you want the wheels off early. Put as much weight on the wings as you can during the ground run, and let ground effect hold you up before true flying speed. Then lower the nose and gain normal airspeed before you climb out of it.

Some airplanes tend to lift off well before VX. In those, let it fly off in ground effect and bring the pitch down to level. Keep the wheels just clear of the runway until the airplane has accelerated to VX.

posts.title: A narrow runway and a low approach
posts.headline: A narrow runway hides how low you really are.
posts.alt: A narrow runway and a low approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A narrow runway hides how low you really are. The picture shows the runway seen obliquely ahead, its paved width visibly narrow with the edges close together and the markings small and crowded; a pale unfilled outline of the usual, wider runway drawn around the real one, so the gap between true edge and outline can be read; ghost outline of the same aeroplane on the normal approach path, at the same distance out and clearly above the solid one; solid aeroplane low on a shallower path, sitting close to the ground short of the threshold. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: You're on short final at a field you've never used, and the picture out the windscreen looks normal.

The runway ahead is narrower than the ones you learned on. A runway narrower than usual creates the illusion of extra height. That is the narrow runway illusion, and it needs nothing more than the width you're looking at. The picture says come down.

Miss it and the approach goes low. Objects along the approach path start to matter, and landing short is the other end of the same mistake. The Aeronautical Information Manual files it at 8-1-5, with the rest of the illusions of flight.
FlightDecide reads the NOTAMs for your destination and flags runway and obstruction notices in the briefing.
Next time you brief an unfamiliar field, look up its runway width and compare it to your home runway.
Check the current CFR before you apply this to a real flight.
teaches: A runway narrower than usual creates the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it actually is.
A pilot who does not recognise the illusion flies a lower-than-normal approach, with the risk of striking objects along the approach path or landing short.
posts.intent: A narrower runway than you are used to makes you feel higher than you are, and the uncorrected result is an approach that is too low.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 17

figure_key.label: NOT THE WIDTH YOU KNOW

article.heading: Why a narrow runway looks higher
paragraphs: Most of your landings happen at one home field, so its runway turns into your ruler. On final you judge your height partly from the runway's shape and size, and you learned that shape at home.
Seen from the air, a runway looks like a trapezoid, a shape wide at your end that narrows toward the far end. On a steady approach at a constant angle, that shape only grows. It doesn't change.

The shape changes when your angle changes. If you get shallow, the runway looks shorter and wider. If you get steep, it looks longer and narrower. That long, thin picture is the one you've learned to read as high.

Now fly to a runway narrower than the one you're used to. It hands you a thin picture from a normal height. The FAA's answer is that a narrower-than-usual runway can make you feel higher than you really are.

figure.caption: A runway narrower than your usual one looks like the right-hand picture even when you're on the right path.
figure.alt: A runway narrower than your usual one looks like the right-hand picture even when you're on the right path.

article.heading: How the wrong picture becomes a low approach
paragraphs: You fly the picture you see. If it tells you you're high, you take off power and lower the nose to come down to where you think you should be.
That correction is the mistake. A pilot who doesn't spot the illusion flies a lower approach than normal, the one the card above shows under the ghost aeroplane.
A low path brings two risks. You can hit objects along the approach path, such as trees or buildings short of the threshold. Or you can land short, touching down before the runway starts.

The same trick works the other way round. A wider-than-usual runway can make you feel low, and the risk then is leveling out high and landing hard or running long. The AIM, at 8-1-5, ranks illusions among the most common factors cited in fatal aircraft accidents.

article.heading: Spotting it before you reach the field
paragraphs: The best defence starts on the ground. Expect visual illusions when you fly to an airport you don't know, and expect them more at night or in bad weather.
Before you go, read the airport diagram and the Chart Supplement, the FAA directory of airport details. They tell you about runway slope, the terrain around it and the lighting.
Width is only one of the things the FAA lists that push an approach low. Several others lead to the same result, so brief them together for any new field.
If you can, look the airport over from the air before you land. And keep your landing skills sharp. The FAA names both as ways to head off these errors.

table.caption: Scenes the FAA says can pull an approach low, and one that pushes it high
columns: What it can make you feel
rows: A lower approach, with the risk of hitting objects or landing short
Leveling out high, landing hard or overshooting
An upsloping runway, upsloping terrain, or both

article.heading: What to trust on final instead
paragraphs: Your eyes still do most of the work on a visual approach, but they need a check that doesn't care how wide the runway is. The FAA says to look at the altimeter often on every approach, day and night.
Use a VASI or PAPI whenever one is there. Both are sets of lights beside the runway that give you a visual reference for the glide path. An electronic glideslope does the same job on instruments.

The aiming point gives you another check. That's the spot on the ground you're descending toward, and on a steady path it seems to stay still. If it creeps up toward the horizon, the point you'll really reach is closer than you think.

Don't stare at one spot. Move your eyes from the aiming point to the horizon, to objects along the runway, to the ground well short of it, and back again. Drifting off the path is easier to catch that way.
Watch out for distraction too. The FAA warns that the chance of an approach accident rises when an emergency or another task pulls you away from your usual routine.

article.heading: Getting back up when you find yourself low
paragraphs: Say the cross-check shows you're low and undershooting. Add power and raise the nose to level off, holding your airspeed as you do it.
When you meet the proper glide path again, reduce power and lower the nose to stay on it. The fix uses power and pitch together, never one on its own.

The tempting mistake is pulling back to stretch the glide with no added power. That raises the angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air, and bleeds off airspeed. You risk a fast sink or a stall close to the ground.
Don't pull the flaps up to fix an undershoot either. It can cost you lift suddenly, raise your sink rate and leave the approach less stable than before.
If you're very low, you may not be able to settle into a stabilized approach, a steady glide at a constant angle, speed and setup toward a chosen point. The normal answer then is a go-around.

posts.title: The black hole approach
posts.headline: Over dark ground you fly lower than you think.
posts.alt: The black hole approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With nothing lit below, you fly lower than intended. The picture shows night side elevation with the lit runway small and far in the right third and the approach entering from the left; solid aeroplane on the lower, shallower path, visibly close to the dark surface short of the field; ghost outline of the same aeroplane on the intended path at the same distance out, clearly above the solid one; completely unlit ground or water between the aeroplane and the threshold, with no towns, roads or scattered lights. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: You turn final over the bay, and the only lights anywhere are the ones on the runway.

Night approaches over unlit terrain or water have a name. The black hole approach. The cues you use to judge height and distance are gone. No roads or rooflines under the nose. Only the runway lights, sitting out there alone.

On a lit approach the picture corrects you the whole way down. Over black ground it never updates. A small sink goes unchallenged. The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge files it with the visual illusions in chapter 17.
FlightDecide reads your destination NOTAMs for the planned window, runway lighting outages included.
If the ground below the approach shows nothing, what is left to tell you how high you are?
teaches: An approach over unlit terrain or water removes the visual cues normally used to judge height and distance.
The result tends toward an approach lower than intended.
posts.intent: With no lit features between you and the runway there is no visual slope information, so the approach is flown on an impression.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 17

article.heading: How you normally judge height
paragraphs: Fly a night approach into a town and the ground keeps telling you where you are. Streetlights, driveways and lit rooftops slide under the nose at a rate you already know. The runway sits inside all that light.

None of it is deliberate. Your eyes compare the runway against the lit ground around it, and against the roads and houses sliding past the side windows. Height and distance come out of that comparison. Take it away and the reading stops.

article.heading: Why dark ground hides the slope
paragraphs: Now put the same runway on the far side of a lake, or behind unlit farmland. The runway edge lights and the threshold lamps are the only light in the windscreen. Between you and them, nothing is lit.

Your peripheral vision, the wide outer part of your sight that reads movement, is getting nothing. The pattern that normally tells you how fast the ground is coming up is absent. So the approach gets flown on the lights alone.

A patch of lights at the far end of the dark is a poor ruler. It is hard to tell how far off it is, and harder to tell what angle you are seeing it from. That is the black hole approach, and it is a picture problem rather than a flying problem.

article.heading: Which way the error goes
paragraphs: The impression is that you are high. Nothing contradicts it, so it sits there while you make the reasonable correction for being high, which is to let the aeroplane down. The path ends up below the one you meant to fly.

Distance drifts the same way. Dark ground with only a few lights on it makes the runway look as though it is receding, further away than it really is. A town beyond the field on higher ground pulls you the same way.

The runway can also look tilted, sloping up or down when it is doing neither. You fly the picture in front of you, because that is all there is. In the worst case it ends in a landing short of the runway.

article.heading: What to fly instead
paragraphs: Find a slope you are not guessing at. A visual approach slope indicator is a light system beside the runway that shows whether you are on the correct angle. An electronic glide slope, the vertical guidance on an instrument approach, does the same job.
With neither on offer, fly the panel. Altitude and rate of descent do not care how dark the ground is. They hold a normal approach when the view will not.

Read the field before you start down. Knowing the layout and where the airport ends means the lights ahead arrive as something you were expecting. Expect the illusion at an unfamiliar airport at night.
If you are unsure how high you are, or where you are against the runway, go around. Doubt is the trigger by itself.

posts.title: Attention narrowing under fatigue
posts.headline: Fatigue narrows your scan before you feel impaired.
posts.alt: Attention narrowing under fatigue: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Fatigue narrows your scan before you feel impaired. The picture shows side elevation of a single-engine aeroplane in profile left of centre, late in the day, with layered ridgelines stepping back to the right into haze; a narrow pale-edged cone of attention opening forward from the cockpit, reaching only one small lit notch of rock at the shoulder of the pass; ghost comparison: a thin unfilled outline of a far wider cone from the same point, spanning nearly the whole forward view, the scan the pilot believes is being flown; terrain inside the narrow cone crisp and readable, everything between its edges and the ghost outline dimmed and softened into haze. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Fourth hour in the airplane, you copy a squawk code and look up to find the heading off the bug.

Fatigue does that. It degrades attention, and it takes away the ability to divide attention between two jobs. Whatever your hands are doing wins. The instrument you were watching a minute ago goes unwatched, and nothing announces it.

You can't feel the narrowing while it's happening. Chapter 2 of the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge covers why fitness gets judged against a written checklist. The same tired brain does the self-assessment, and it reports back that everything is fine.
FlightDecide reads the TAFs and NOTAMs across your whole planned window, so late-day workload is visible early.
On a long day, the checklist is the only honest opinion in the cockpit.
teaches: Fatigue degrades attention and the ability to divide it between tasks.
The degradation is difficult to self-assess, which is why a checklist rather than a feeling is used to judge fitness.
posts.intent: Fatigue narrows the field of attention before it feels like impairment, so the scan stops covering what you think it covers.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 2

article.heading: Why the scan shrinks
paragraphs: Attention is not one supply that you either have or do not have. Part of it is the work of splitting attention across several jobs that all need some. Fatigue degrades both of those.
The task in front of you holds on to its share. The one you only glance at loses turns, and the gap between glances gets longer.
Nothing goes dark when that happens. The part of the view you take in gets narrower, and it narrows around whatever you are working on.
You go heads down to set up the approach. When you look up, the airplane has been in a slow left turn for longer than you would have allowed.

article.heading: Why self-assessment misses it
paragraphs: The degradation is difficult to judge from inside your own head. The judgement about whether you are fit to fly runs on the faculty the fatigue is degrading.
There is also nothing that presents as missing. A narrow scan returns a sharp read of a small area, and it reports nothing at all about the rest.
So the picture you hold of your own coverage stays wide while the coverage itself shrinks. You are working from the version you had on a rested morning flight.
Traffic is the plain case. It sits in the windscreen, outside the band you are sampling, and leaves nothing behind for you to remember afterwards.

article.heading: Where it costs the most
paragraphs: Workload is not level from taxi to shutdown. The tasks increase sharply in the landing phase, and that phase demands more precision and attention than cruise does.
It is also the phase that asks you to hold several jobs at once. You watch airspeed and path while you change configuration, work the radio and look for other airplanes.

The accident record is concentrated in the same places. Landing accounts for 24.1 percent of general aviation accidents and takeoff for 23.4 percent. Approximately 80 percent of all aviation accidents are related to human factors.
The hours that tire you out come before the approach, not after it. Your narrowest scan of the day and the busiest flying of the day arrive together.

article.heading: What to use instead
paragraphs: Fitness gets judged against a written checklist because the feeling is not evidence. A list asks you things you answer by counting and by looking at a clock.
Personal minimums work the same way. You set them in advance and build them into habit, so the number exists before you have to apply it.
A written answer will never tell you that you are sharp. It tells you whether you are inside a limit you drew while you could still see well enough to draw it.

posts.title: Stall speed rising with bank angle
posts.headline: Steepen a level turn and your stall speed rises.
posts.alt: Stall speed rising with bank angle: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A steeper level turn raises your stall speed. The picture shows a rendered single-engine aircraft heeled hard over in a steep turn, wings near sixty degrees of bank; the nose held on the horizon so the steep turn reads as level, not descending; a pale ghost of the same aircraft in a shallow bank, wings close to level; a thin level reference line joining solid aircraft and ghost at the same altitude. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Halfway around the steep turn the horn chirps, and the airspeed needle hasn't moved.

The wing is holding you up and hauling you around the corner at the same time. In a level turn, load factor grows with bank angle. Stall speed follows the square root of that load. Same airplane, higher number.

That number never shows up on the panel. The needle reads the same as it did wings level, so the margin feels unchanged. It has shrunk. The Airplane Flying Handbook works through steep turns in chapter 5.
FlightDecide computes the weight and balance for your planned load, so the gross weight behind your published stall speeds is a number you already have.
Next steep turns with your instructor, note the speed where the buffet starts and compare it to the wings level figure.
teaches: In a level turn load factor increases with bank angle.
Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor, so a 60 degree level turn doubles the load and raises the stall speed by about 41 percent.
posts.intent: A level turn raises load factor and the stall speed rises with the square root of it, so a steep turn stalls at a higher speed.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 5

figure_key.points_at: The needle of the small round accelerometer face at lower right.

article.heading: Why a steep turn stalls sooner
paragraphs: Picture yourself holding altitude at a steady airspeed and rolling into a 60 degree bank. The airspeed has not changed. Yet the airplane is now closer to a stall than it was a moment ago.

The reason is the extra work the wing is doing. In a level turn it has to hold up the airplane's weight and pull it around the corner at the same time. The steeper the bank, the harder the wing works.
That extra work has a name, load factor, and the stall speed rises with it. At 60 degrees of bank, the FAA's Airplane Flying Handbook puts the rise at 41 percent over the wings level stall speed.

article.heading: What load factor means
paragraphs: Load factor is the load the wing carries compared with the airplane's weight. Flying straight and level, the wing carries exactly the weight, and that is 1G. At 2G the wing is carrying twice the weight.
In a turn, the wing's lift tilts with the airplane. Part of it now points toward the center of the turn and pulls you around. Only the rest is left pointing up against the weight.

To stay level, you ask the wing for more lift in total. The more you bank, the more of that lift goes sideways, and the more total lift you need. So in a level turn, load factor grows with bank angle.

In a coordinated, level 60 degree bank, the load factor is 2G. Coordinated means the ball in the slip/skid indicator is centered. The wing is now holding up twice the airplane's weight at the same airspeed.

figure.caption: In the bank, the tilted lift has to grow to twice the weight so that its upward part still matches the weight.
figure.alt: In the bank, the tilted lift has to grow to twice the weight so that its upward part still matches the weight.

article.heading: How the square root sets the number
paragraphs: Stall speed does not rise at the same rate as load factor. It rises with the square root of the load factor. So when the load doubles, the stall speed goes up by 41 percent rather than doubling.
That softens the jump, but only a little. A 41 percent rise is a big change to a number that is easy to treat as fixed.

Take the wings level stall speed you learned for your own airplane. In a coordinated, level 60 degree bank, the stall comes at that figure plus 41 percent. The handbook gives no stall speed for any one airplane, so do the sum with yours.

table.caption: The same airplane at the same airspeed, wings level and in a level 60 degree turn.

article.heading: Why the stall follows angle of attack
paragraphs: To make that extra lift at the same airspeed, you raise the angle of attack. Angle of attack is the angle at which the wing's chord, a straight line from leading to trailing edge, meets the oncoming air.
As that angle grows, lift grows and so does drag. Each wing has a limit to that angle. Beyond it, the airflow separates from the top surface, lift drops and drag climbs. That is a stall.
The handbook is firm here. A stall comes from exceeding that limiting angle, not from a lack of airspeed. Stall speed is only the airspeed at which you reach the limit under one set of conditions.

In a 2G turn you are already holding a higher angle of attack than you did wings level. You sit closer to the limit, and so closer to the higher stall speed. That is why the handbook says you can stall at any airspeed, in any attitude and at any power setting.

Load factor is one of several things that set stall speed. Gross weight, center of gravity and flap setting move it too. Stall speed is not a constant, and the handbook wants you to understand what moves it.

article.heading: What changes when you are already slow
paragraphs: In slow flight practice you fly a target speed just above the stall warning. The handbook suggests 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed. That margin is measured against a wings level stall.
At that speed, any further increase in angle of attack or load factor, or any cut in power, brings a stall warning. Rolling into a steeper bank is exactly that kind of load factor increase.
Put the two numbers side by side. Your margin was 5 to 10 knots over the 1G stall speed. Steepen the bank and the stall speed itself climbs toward the speed you are flying.
Reduced airspeeds are normal on takeoff and departure, and on approach and landing. Those are also the phases flown close to the ground. A turn there adds load factor to a speed that was already low.

article.heading: What the airplane tells you first
paragraphs: A stall warning comes before the stall itself. It shows up as buffet, a shaking you feel through the airframe, or as the stall horn sounding.
The handbook says to react to and correct for any stall indication. A stall can lead to loss of control if the angle of attack is not reduced.

The stall speeds you learn for your airplane are 1G figures for one weight and configuration. In a steep level turn, the warning arrives at a speed that would give you room to spare wings level. Knowing why keeps it from being a surprise.
The aim, in slow flight and in turns, is to maneuver without setting off the stall warning at all. Knowing that 60 degrees of bank means 2G and a 41 percent higher stall speed is what lets you do it.

posts.title: Losing the headwind on final
posts.headline: A decreasing headwind costs airspeed and drops you below the path.
posts.alt: Losing the headwind on final: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A decreasing headwind costs airspeed and drops you below the path. The picture shows two wind layers divided by a soft shear seam: long streamlines above, short stubby ones below; a dashed intended glidepath running straight down to the runway threshold; the solid aircraft sitting beneath that dashed path, just after crossing the seam; a pale ghost of the same aircraft still on the dashed path at the same point along final. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Headwind loss on final arrives late in the approach, where you have the least altitude to spare.

On final you are low and committed to a path. The wing knows only the air moving over it right now. Pattern altitude is history. A headwind that weakens as you descend hands you a sink you never asked for.

It is easy to read the sag as your own flying. The air changed. The Airplane Flying Handbook covers this in its approach and landing chapter. The speed does come back. You are lower than you planned by the time it does.
FlightDecide reads the wind lines in your TAF for the planned window, including a low level wind shear group when the forecast carries one.
One sentence worth carrying down final: the speed sagged because the air changed, and the airplane is already going low.
teaches: A decreasing headwind with descent produces a momentary loss of indicated airspeed.
The aircraft sinks below the intended path, and getting the airspeed back does not by itself return it to the path.
The pilot must recover the path, promptly adding power and adjusting pitch to correct for the wind's effect on the descent.
posts.intent: Descending out of a stronger wind into a weaker one costs airspeed, and the aircraft sinks below the path while it recovers.

article.heading: What it looks like on final
paragraphs: You are established on final, trimmed and descending toward your aiming point. Then the airspeed sags without you touching the throttle or the yoke. A moment later the view through the windscreen says you are lower than you planned.
It is natural to blame your own flying and start chasing the needle. In this case the cause is the air. The headwind you had higher up has grown weaker as you came down.

That change is wind shear, a sudden change in wind speed or direction over a short distance, usually from one height to another. It can be reported, but it often goes undetected until you fly into it.
Moderate turbulence usually brings variations in indicated airspeed too. This is different. It is a loss tied to your descent through one layer of air into another.

article.heading: Why a weaker headwind costs airspeed
paragraphs: Your wing only responds to the air flowing over it. Indicated airspeed, the speed on your airspeed indicator, measures that flow. It says nothing about your speed over the ground.

In a strong headwind, the air is streaming toward you as you fly into it. Descend into a layer where that stream is slower, and the airplane at first carries its old motion. Less air now meets the wing, so indicated airspeed drops.
Nothing is wrong with the engine or the trim. The airplane has simply not caught up with the new air yet. That lag is why the loss is momentary.
The Aviation Weather Handbook notes that shear causes abrupt changes in an airplane's horizontal movement. On final, a weakening headwind is one of those changes, and you feel it as lost airspeed.

article.heading: Why getting the speed back is not enough
paragraphs: While the speed is low, the wing makes less lift than it did a moment before. The airplane sinks faster than your planned descent. The handbooks tie slow airspeed and too little lift directly to an airplane settling.
Your glidepath, the planned line from you down to the aiming point, stays where it was. The airplane has dropped under it. As the airplane settles into the new air, the airspeed returns.
Getting that speed back does not lift you back to the line. You come out of the sag at the right speed and the wrong height. The gap stays until you fix it.
This is why the timing matters. Low level shear is especially hazardous because the airplane is close to the ground. On final there is very little height left to lose.

figure.caption: The airspeed comes back without any help from you, but the height lost during the dip stays lost until you add power.
figure.alt: The airspeed comes back without any help from you, but the height lost during the dip stays lost until you add power.

article.heading: How to get back on the path
paragraphs: The recovery is about the height as much as the speed. Add power promptly, and adjust pitch to correct for what the wind did to your descent. Waiting for the speed to return by itself leaves you low.

Pitch alone will not do it. The Airplane Flying Handbook explains that when you are slow, raising the nose cuts airspeed further and greatly steepens the descent. Raise it too far and the airplane settles rapidly on too little lift.
The same handbook warns never to try to stretch a glide to reach a spot. Pulling back to hold the path without adding power is exactly that stretch.

It helps to know your margin. In its accuracy approaches, the handbook uses 1.3 VSO on final, where VSO is the stall speed with the airplane configured to land. A sag in airspeed comes straight out of that margin.
Correcting the wind's effect on your descent is the real goal. The airspeed is only the first thing the shear took from you.

article.heading: What makes the wind change near the ground
paragraphs: Wind that changes sharply at low height has many sources. The handbook lists terrain, temperature inversions, sea breezes, frontal systems and strong surface winds.

A temperature inversion is a layer where the air gets warmer with height instead of cooler. Inversions often sit in the lowest few thousand feet after the ground cools overnight. Strong wind shear often forms across them.

Thunderstorms add their own version. The gust front, the leading edge of wind flowing out from a storm, often runs as far as 15 mi ahead of the rain. It changes the surface wind rapidly and sometimes drastically.
A line of dust or debris along the ground, or spray across water, often marks where the gust front is at the surface.

article.heading: How big a change counts as shear
paragraphs: The handbook puts numbers on low level wind shear that does not come from storms. It is a change of 10 kt or more for every 100 ft of height.

That change has to happen in a layer more than 200 ft thick, within 2,000 ft of the surface. The handbook's practice patterns begin at approximately 1,000 feet above the ground, so your whole final sits inside that band.

This kind of shear is commonly tied to passing fronts, temperature inversions and strong upper-level winds, meaning greater than 25 kt. Some references also use the term severe wind shear, with thresholds of their own.

Severe wind shear can also mean shear that exceeds what the airplane is able to do. Wind shear can affect a flight at any altitude. Near the ground, it has long been counted a serious hazard on takeoff and approach.

posts.title: A temperature inversion trapping haze
posts.headline: The inversion that smooths the air also traps the haze below.
posts.alt: A temperature inversion trapping haze: an illustrated diagram for pilots. The inversion that smooths the air also traps the haze below. The picture shows a valley filled with dense haze whose top is cut off along one ruler-straight horizontal line; clean transparent air above that line with distant ranges still crisp and edged; a smoke column from a chimney that climbs vertically, stops dead at the line, and spreads sideways into a long level sheet; a small profile aircraft flying at the top of the haze with wings dead level. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Temperature inversions are stable layers, and stable air is what keeps the haze from clearing.

Vertical motion is what carries smoke and haze away. A stable layer has none, so it collects in the air you are looking through. Stability does all of it. The Aviation Weather Handbook covers inversions in chapter 18.

A smooth ride is easy to read as good conditions. It reports on mixing. With mixing suppressed, the haze underneath has nothing to lift it out and nowhere to go. Smooth air is what the trap feels like from inside.
FlightDecide reads the TAFs for your planned window and shows the forecast visibility and haze in a briefing you can check against raw data.
If the ride goes glassy and the horizon turns milky, one layer is doing both.

teaches: A temperature inversion is a stable layer that suppresses vertical mixing.
Because mixing is suppressed, haze and smoke concentrate below the inversion while the air within it is smooth.
posts.intent: Smooth air and poor visibility arrive together, because the inversion that stops the mixing also traps what is in the air.
