article.heading: What a temperature inversion is
paragraphs: Air normally gets colder as you climb away from the ground. An inversion is a layer where that order turns over, with warmer air lying above cooler air.

Forecasters judge a layer by what happens to a small parcel of air pushed up into it. Inside an inversion, that parcel arrives colder and denser than the air around it. Being heavier, it settles back to the level it came from.
A profile like that is classed as absolute stability. Every parcel you could test in the layer resists being lifted, whether it is saturated or not.

article.heading: Why the air stops mixing
paragraphs: Stability is a property of the air you are flying through, and it decides whether vertical motion grows or dies. A stable layer answers every upward nudge with a push back down. Motion that starts inside it does not get far.
Vertical motion is how low air and high air trade places. With that exchange shut off, the air under the layer stays under the layer.
The ride smooths out for the same reason. Bumps in the low levels are parcels rising and sinking, and a stable layer does not allow them to.

article.heading: Why the haze stays below
paragraphs: Haze and smoke go where the air goes. Carried upward, they spread through a deep column and thin out. Held down, they stay in the shallow slice of air near the surface.

Under an inversion the second case applies. Whatever was already in the low air remains there, and anything added to it joins the same shallow layer. Concentration climbs because the volume available to it has stopped growing.
That slice is the air you look through in the pattern and on a low cross country. How far you can see is set by how much has gathered in it, not by how clear the sky is overhead.

article.heading: What the smooth ride reports
paragraphs: Comfort in the cockpit is a readout of how little the air is moving up and down. It carries no information about what that same stillness has collected underneath you.
Both conditions come from one property of one layer. One layer damped the turbulence and stopped the ventilation at the same time.
Plan for the visibility to be poorest on the mornings the air feels best. A glassy climb out of a valley is a reason to check the reported visibility again, not a reason to relax about it.

article.heading: When the trap lets go
paragraphs: Stability follows how fast temperature falls with height. Steepen that fall and stability drops.

Sun on the ground warms the air in contact with it, which steepens the profile from below. Once the heating has worked up through the layer, vertical motion returns. The load of haze then has a much deeper column to spread through.
Heating is not the only lever. Most changes in stability come from air moving in from somewhere else, so a layer can be built or broken by what arrives aloft.

posts.title: Lee-side downdraft
posts.headline: The air can sink faster than you can climb.
posts.alt: Lee-side downdraft: an illustrated diagram for pilots. The air can sink faster than you can climb.
caption: Lee-side downdraft: pitched up at climb power, an aircraft can still be losing height.

You plan a ridge crossing around climb performance. Descending air on the lee side can take that margin back, and FAA-H-8083-28 chapter 16 covers that flow. The margin goes first. The height goes next.
It is easy to read the attitude as proof of a climb. Pitch and power are inputs. The altimeter is the output. A steady nose-up picture can sit on top of a descending trend for the whole crossing.
FlightDecide computes the weight and balance for your planned flight window, which is one input to the climb performance you will have on the day.
If the nose is up and the altimeter is unwinding, believe the altimeter.
teaches: On the lee side of a ridge the air can be descending, and it can descend faster than a light aircraft climbs.
So a climb attitude does not guarantee a climb: the aircraft can be pitched up, at climb power, and still losing height.
posts.intent: air spilling down the downwind side of a ridge can descend faster than a light aircraft can climb, even at a climb attitude

article.heading: Why the air sinks there
paragraphs: The wind does not stop at the ridge. When the air is stable and the wind is strong, the whole layer gets lifted over the top.
Gravity pulls it back down, and it does not stop at the level it came from. Momentum then carries it well below that height before it begins to rise once more.
That descending stretch is the lee-side downdraft. It sits on the downwind side, right where you are still trying to climb.

article.heading: Climbing through air that is falling
paragraphs: Your climb rate is measured against the air around you, not against the ground. When that air is sinking faster than you climb, your height falls while the wing keeps climbing.
A light aircraft does not have a large climb rate to spend. Set a descending air mass against it and the sum can come out below zero. You sink.
Nothing in the cockpit picture changes while this happens. The attitude holds and the airspeed sits where you put it. Only the vertical speed and the terrain ahead tell you anything is wrong.

article.heading: When a ridge makes waves
paragraphs: A wave needs strong wind and stable air upwind of the ridge. Take away either one and the air behaves in another way.

Weak wind can leave the mountains acting as a dam, holding the air back on the upwind side. Unstable air that carries enough moisture tends to build convective cloud rather than a smooth wave. Neither of those is the lee-side case.
Season matters. Late autumn through early spring is when the large-scale winds run strongest, and that is when the worst mountain wind events show up.

article.heading: Where the sinking air sits
paragraphs: The descending air is part of a wave, so it repeats. Past the first trough the air swings back up and then overshoots once more. The oscillation fades downstream.

That gives you bands of sinking air separated by bands of rising air. Crossing them, the vertical speed swings one way and then the other. One good climb through a rising band does not mean the sink is behind you.
The handbook names two shapes for this. A vertically propagating mountain wave and a trapped lee wave can both be present, and each can be hazardous. The name matters less than the sink.

article.heading: What you might see first
paragraphs: Sometimes the flow announces itself. Lenticular cloud and blowing dust mark mountain flow that is under way. Rotor cloud under the wave is another sign.
The handbook is direct about the other case, where severe wind events happen with little or no visual warning. A clear sky over a ridge is not a promise that the lee side is quiet.
The ridge bends the wind and breaks it into eddies at the same time. Those run from a few centimeters to tens or hundreds of kilometers across. The ride through them can be smooth or violent.

posts.title: Wind correction angle
posts.headline: Line up with where you are going, not where you are pointing.
posts.alt: Wind correction angle: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Line up with where you are going, not where you are pointing.
caption: Wind correction angle is what keeps your track on the extended centreline in a crosswind.

In a crosswind your heading and your track over the ground are two different things. The angle between them is the wind correction angle. On final, hold it into the wind. The track then stays down the extended centreline. The crab comes out before touchdown, so the aeroplane lands with its longitudinal axis on the runway.
It is easy to read a nose pointed straight at the runway as lined up. You drift when the correction is missing. Chapter 16 of FAA-H-8083-25 lays out the same wind triangle for cross country legs.
FlightDecide pulls wind direction and speed from the TAF for your planned window, then scores it in the go/no-go advisor.
On the next crosswind final, notice how far off the runway heading your nose sits while the track stays straight.
teaches: In a crosswind an aircraft's heading and its track over the ground are different, and the angle between them is the wind correction angle.
On the approach, holding a wind correction angle into the wind is what keeps the track along the extended centreline.
An aircraft that points straight at the runway in a crosswind, with no correction applied, drifts downwind of the centreline.
Taking the crab out the instant before touchdown aligns the axis with the runway, but aileron into the wind stops the drift.
posts.intent: in a crosswind the aeroplane's nose points off to one side while its path over the ground stays on the centreline

article.heading: Why your nose and your path disagree
paragraphs: Picture yourself flying at 90 knots with a 10 knot wind blowing from right to left. Through the air you still move forward at 90 knots. But the air is moving too, so it carries you 10 nautical miles to the left every hour.

Double your speed to 180 knots and that sideways drift does not shrink. You still move 10 nautical miles left each hour. Once you are airborne, you go wherever the air mass goes, whichever way the nose points.

That leaves you with two directions. Your heading is the way the nose points. Your track is the path you actually trace over the ground. In a crosswind they differ, and the angle between them is the wind correction angle.

article.heading: How far to turn into the wind
paragraphs: To fly a straight line over the ground, you angle the nose into the wind. Point far enough upwind and the sideways push is cancelled. Your track then runs straight to where you want to go.

Three things set the size of that angle. They are the wind speed, the angle between the wind and your longitudinal axis (the line from nose to tail), and your airspeed. More wind needs a bigger angle, and more airspeed needs a smaller one.
The handbook gives a worked pair. At 100 knots with 20 knots of wind straight from the side, you turn 12° into the wind. Halve the wind to 10 knots and the correction halves to six degrees.

A boat crossing a river works the same way. The captain angles the bow upstream so the boat's own motion matches the current pushing it downstream. A slower boat or a faster river needs a bigger angle.

table.caption: Wind correction angle for a wind directly from the side, from the handbook's example.

article.heading: What happens if you point at the runway
paragraphs: Now put yourself on final with the wind from the left. The runway sits dead ahead, so aiming the nose straight at it feels right. With no correction applied, the wind moves you sideways and you drift downwind of the centreline.

That drift builds up to the speed of the crosswind component, the part of the wind acting across your path. A wind directly from the side drifts you at its full speed. A wind at 45°, halfway between the nose and the side, drifts you at just over 70 percent of its speed.

So a nose aimed at the threshold tells you nothing about your track. Scan between references far ahead and close to the aeroplane. That is how you see whether you are holding the line or sliding off it.

article.heading: Holding the crab down final
paragraphs: The crab method, holding your heading off into the wind, puts the wind correction angle to work directly. You turn toward the wind until your wings-level ground track lines up with the runway centreline. The nose now sits off to the upwind side while you track straight down the extended centreline.
The wind rarely stays the same all the way down. Make small heading changes as needed to keep that alignment. You are flying the track, and the heading is whatever it takes to hold it.
The handbook calls the crab the easier method to keep up on final. The price comes at the bottom. Taking the crab out needs judgment and precise timing.

article.heading: Taking the crab out before touchdown
paragraphs: Tyres do not like landing sideways. When a loaded tyre's path and its heading differ, that difference is called the cornering angle, and it creates a side load. As little as 10° of cornering angle produces a side load equal to half the weight the tyre carries.

So you hold the crab until the instant before touchdown. Then you use rudder to swing the longitudinal axis into line with the direction you are moving. Straighten up too early or too late and the wheels meet the runway with a side load.

The round out, the flare just above the runway, is flown much like a normal one. You keep applying crosswind correction as needed to stop any drift. As you slow, the controls lose effect, so the correction you are holding becomes too small unless you add more.

article.heading: The wing-low method holds both together
paragraphs: The handbook recommends the wing-low method, also called a sideslip, in most cases. It keeps your track and your longitudinal axis on the centreline all the way to the ground. There is no heading change to time at the last moment.

First you use rudder to line the heading up with the runway. That leaves you in an uncorrected crosswind, so you start to drift. You then bank into the wind with aileron, just enough to cancel the drift.

More bank moves you upwind and less lets you slide downwind. Adjust both controls until you are tracking the centreline with the nose already straight. On a long final you can crab first and change smoothly to wing-low before the round out.
Keep the upwind wing down through the round out. Level the wings and the drift comes back, so you touch down moving sideways. Done well, the upwind main wheel touches first.

In a strong crosswind you lower the upwind wing further and need a lot of opposite rudder to stop the turn. If full opposite rudder still cannot hold the nose straight, the wind is too strong for that runway. Land on a better-aligned runway there or at an alternate.

figure.caption: Both methods keep you on the centreline, but the crab angles the nose into the wind while the wing-low method banks into it with the nose straight.
figure.alt: Both methods keep you on the centreline, but the crab angles the nose into the wind while the wing-low method banks into it with the nose straight.

posts.title: Density altitude
posts.headline: Thin air lengthens your takeoff and flattens your climb.
posts.alt: Density altitude: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Thin air lengthens your takeoff and flattens your climb.
caption: Density altitude takes thrust from the propeller and lift from the wing, and the runway does not grow.

Heat and elevation both thin the air. The field that felt long at seven in the morning is a different field at three in the afternoon. Your loading has not changed and neither has your technique. The ground roll grows anyway.

It is easy to treat runway length as the whole question. The climb gradient available is reduced on that same afternoon, and the rising ground past the departure end is still there. FAA-H-8083-25 chapter 11 has the performance side of this.
FlightDecide reads the TAF for your planned window and the weight and balance you entered, then scores both in one advisory.
After the longer ground roll, what is the other half of a density altitude problem?
teaches: Heat and elevation both thin the air, and thin air reduces the thrust the propeller makes and the lift the wing makes at a given speed.
Takeoff distance therefore grows with density altitude while the aircraft, its weight and the pilot's technique are all unchanged.
Rising terrain beyond the runway matters more on a thin-air day, because the climb gradient available is reduced at the same time as the ground roll is lengthened.
posts.intent: the same aeroplane uses far more runway to get airborne when the air is thin than when it is dense

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 11

article.heading: What thin air does to the same aeroplane
paragraphs: Picture one aeroplane at one weight, flown by one pilot, on two different days. On the first it lifts off with plenty of runway left. On the second it rolls and rolls before it will fly.
The difference is the air. Air density, the amount of air packed into a given space, sets how hard the air pushes back on the propeller and the wing.

Pilots put that density into a single number called density altitude. It is the height in the standard atmosphere, a reference model of pressure and temperature, where air is as dense as today's air. Your aeroplane performs as if it were at that height, whatever the field elevation says.
A high density altitude means thin air, and performance drops. A low density altitude means dense air, and performance improves.

article.heading: How height and heat each thin the air
paragraphs: The higher you go, the less air there is above you pressing down. With less pressure on it, air spreads out, so each cubic foot holds less of it.

The standard atmosphere puts sea level at 29.92 inHg, inches of mercury, and 15.0 °C. By 5,000 feet the standard pressure is down to 24.89 inHg. That is why Denver starts with thinner air than New Orleans before the weather has any say.
Heat thins the air as well. Warm air expands and takes up more room, so the same space holds less of it. From one airport to another across the country, temperature is the biggest driver of density.

Pressure altitude is what your altimeter reads when you set it to 29.92 inHg. The FAA weather handbook takes a pressure altitude of 10,000 ft with the air at 20 °C. The density altitude there is 12,700 ft.
Humidity adds a little on top. Water vapour is lighter than dry air, so moist air is less dense, though the handbooks treat the effect as small.

figure.caption: The same space holds less air when it is warmer or higher, which leaves the propeller and wing less to work with.
figure.alt: The same space holds less air when it is warmer or higher, which leaves the propeller and wing less to work with.

table.caption: Standard pressure and temperature both fall as you climb, from FAA-H-8083-25 Figure 11-2.

article.heading: Why the ground roll grows
paragraphs: Thin air hits the aeroplane in three ways at once. The engine takes in less air, so it makes less power. The propeller has less air to push back, so it makes less thrust.
The wing loses out too. Lift comes from air pressing on the wing, and lighter air presses less at the same speed.

Here is the part that catches pilots out. Your airspeed indicator shows nothing unusual, and you rotate at the usual indicated airspeed. Your true airspeed, your real speed through the air, is higher.

A higher true airspeed means a higher groundspeed at liftoff. So the aeroplane has to run faster along the runway before it will fly. It does that with less thrust to speed it up, which adds still more runway.
None of this needs a heavier load or a sloppier technique. The aeroplane and the pilot are exactly as they were. Only the air is different.

article.heading: How much longer, in the handbook's example
paragraphs: The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25, works through one case. The altimeter, set to 29.92 inHg, shows a pressure altitude of 5,000 feet.

On a standard temperature day, the example has the POH, the pilot's operating handbook, calling for a ground run of 790 feet. On a standard day, pressure altitude and density altitude sit at the same level.
Now make the day 20 °C warmer than standard. The warm air expands, and the density altitude rises above 7,000 feet. The ground run in the example comes out closer to 1,000 feet.
Same runway, same aeroplane, same pilot. Those are the handbook's example figures, and your own aeroplane's numbers come from the manufacturer's performance charts.

table.caption: One pressure altitude, two temperatures, from the example in FAA-H-8083-25 chapter 11.
rows: 20 °C above standard, at 5,000 ft pressure altitude

article.heading: Why rising ground past the runway matters more
paragraphs: Getting off the ground is only half the job. Once airborne, you still have to climb away from whatever lies past the departure end.

Thin air cuts your rate of climb, because the engine and propeller have less to give. You also fly the climb at the usual indicated airspeed, which is a faster true airspeed. Covering more ground each minute while gaining less height gives a shallower climb angle.

On a hot day at a high field, both effects land together. You leave the ground later, further down the runway, then climb more gently from that later point. Hills you clear easily on a cold morning sit closer to your path.
So a runway that is long enough is not the same as a departure that works. The climb out over the ground beyond it needs checking against the same conditions.

article.heading: Working out density altitude before you go
paragraphs: You start with pressure altitude. Set 29.92 inHg on the altimeter and read it, or correct field elevation for the current altimeter setting.
The handbook's worked case is a sea level field with an altimeter setting of 29.7. Its table gives a correction of 205 feet, so the pressure altitude is 205 feet.
Next you correct that for temperature. A flight computer does it from pressure altitude and outside air temperature. The density altitude chart in chapter 11 does the same job on paper.
There is no rule of thumb or chart for humidity. On a warm, damp day, expect less performance than your dry-air numbers show.
